title: How Far Will AI Go?
description: Would you ever call AI your friend? 🤖 Plenty of people are dubious about AI. Who controls it? Can we trust its answers? What happens to the things we share? But imagine an AI that remembers your interests, gets your humour and is there for a conversation at 2am. Would you see it as a useful tool—or start to feel a friendship? And how far could this go? Would you want AI helping with everyday decisions, keeping you company, or becoming part of your home? For the Deaf community, what would make an AI companion worth using? The way it communicates? How well it understands Deaf culture? Or knowing exactly what happens to your conversations? A convincing answer isn’t always a correct one. And sounding caring raises another question: does it actually understand you? Where do you stand—curious, cautious, completely against it, or already chatting with AI regularly?

title: The Week the Cracks in the AI Trade Grew Deeper

title: Chainalysis says external actor used offensive AI agentic techniques in breach
description: 📅 October 30, 2026 • Source: Chainalysis Chainalysis, a blockchain analytics company known for its KYT compliance platform and the Reactor investigation tool, reported on October 30 that it identified an external actor who used what the company describes as offensive agentic techniques to obtain unauthorized access to some of its systems and internal tools. The company said customers have been notified. The description matters for the wider industry: the incident is attributed not to a single exploit but to AI agents performing coordinated multi-step actions against the infrastructure of an analytics vendor. What the company says happened. According to Chainalysis, the actor reached a limited set of non-sensitive customer data. The company lists four categories: user identifiers, full names, email addresses and role labels within customer organizations. At the same time, the company states it found no signs of access to the content of investigations, to authentication credentials or to session tokens, which form the working core of the platform. Chainalysis says it is patching the identified vulnerabilities and hardening its systems with external cybersecurity experts. Two caveats frame the report: the company did not disclose technical details of the attack vector and did not name the actor, so the account of the techniques rests on the company's own statements rather than independent verification. Overview coverage likewise relays the company's formulations without an independent assessment. IMPACT For compliance teams running KYT and for investigators working in Reactor, the statement implies that case files and credentials were not affected, while contact-level customer information was exposed. Customers can expect vendor notifications and should track follow-up messages clarifying which records were involved. Beyond this case, the incident signals that agentic AI is being used offensively against infrastructure providers, which extends threat modeling for analytics and compliance platforms beyond the familiar scenario of a data leak toward agent-driven access paths. The picture may change as technical detail is published, and the company notes the investigation is ongoing with external specialists involved in remediation. Chainalysis also addressed public speculation: the company says the incident is fully separate from the recent crypto theft at the Binance exchange and should not be linked to it. For customers, the practical steps are to review what data of theirs was in scope, apply guidance from the vendor notifications and monitor for updated disclosures. The event is likely to be cited in security planning as an early documented case in which a vendor named offensive agentic techniques as the access method.
